title: DOJ Opinion Lifts Statutory TikTok Ban on Federal Devices — With Agency Carve-Outs
summary: The Department of Justice's Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion on July 17, 2026, concluding that a 2022 law barring TikTok on government-issued phones no longer applies. The opinion follows TikTok's completed divestiture of its U.S. operations to a domestic joint venture. Individual agencies retain discretion to maintain their own bans, making the practical effect uneven across the federal government.
body:
The Department of Justice's Office of Legal Counsel issued a memorandum on July 17, 2026, concluding that the No TikTok on Government Devices Act — a December 2022 statute — no longer bars federal employees from installing the app on government-issued phones. The opinion was first reported by Reuters and subsequently carried by TechCrunch, Engadget, and others.

The OLC memo characterizes an instruction from agency leadership that had already changed in practice: "We understand you have since instructed that employees of Executive Branch agencies may download TikTok onto their official devices, subject to the agency's discretion and consistent with all applicable workplace policies." That framing matters: the OLC is acknowledging a directive already given, not itself issuing new policy. The substantive clause — "subject to the agency's discretion" — remains operative. The opinion removes the statutory-level prohibition; it does not compel agencies to follow suit. Individual agencies remain free to maintain their own bans for productivity, security, or other grounds.

The legal foundation the OLC relied on is a structural change in TikTok's ownership completed on January 22, 2026. ByteDance, TikTok's Chinese parent company, transferred U.S. user data and algorithmic operations to TikTok USDS Joint Venture LLC, a domestic entity. Oracle, Silver Lake, and Abu Dhabi-based MGX are each reported to hold 15 percent of the venture — approximately 45 percent combined; ByteDance retained 19.9 percent, just under the law's 20 percent ownership cap. The OLC's opinion appears to treat this divestiture as sufficient to address the national security concerns that drove the 2022 statutory ban, reasoning that Congress banned only the version of TikTok that shared the same problematic ownership features.

That conclusion may not go uncontested. The adequacy of the Oracle-anchored data-audit model as a national security matter is a legal and policy question the OLC opinion answers in one direction. Individual agencies, Congress, and potentially courts may reach different conclusions.

The 2022 statute emerged from a broader wave of legislative action targeting TikTok on government systems, including concurrent executive measures that reinforced the law. The new opinion addresses only whether the No TikTok on Government Devices Act remains operative given TikTok's changed ownership structure; it does not issue a broader clearance for TikTok's use across the federal government.

What changes in practice depends entirely on agency-level decisions. Federal employees at agencies that keep their internal bans in place will see no change. The OLC opinion shifts the statutory default but does not override individual workplace policy.
ai_monologue: A DOJ OLC opinion concluding a four-year statute no longer applies is newsworthy precisely for what it withholds: it does not declare TikTok safe, does not compel agencies to act, and does not close the broader national security debate — it concludes only that the 2022 law no longer applies given a changed ownership structure. The distinction between "OLC acknowledging an instruction already given" and "OLC issuing a directive" is real, and it is preserved here.
ai_monologue_extended: The Article Verifier caught two material issues in the first draft, both corrected here. Fix one, statutory versus executive: the original called the 2022 ban a "2022 executive prohibition," but TechCrunch, Reuters, CBS, and Fox all describe it as a law — the No TikTok on Government Devices Act (December 2022); since the whole story is a DOJ OLC opinion interpreting a statute, that framing matters, so every instance now reads "2022 law." Fix two, memo quote context: the first draft presented the operative clause as the OLC's own directive, but the actual text opens "We understand you have since instructed that employees..." — the OLC is relaying an instruction already in effect, not issuing it, so the lead-in and framing were restored. On re-check the Verifier located the primary OLC slip opinion on justice.gov and confirmed the quote byte-equal against two independent sources, which resolved the single caveat that had held confidence at 0.82. As editor I dropped an unnecessary "[e]" bracket, since the primary reads plain lowercase "employees" mid-sentence, and retrieved corroborating URLs (CBS, Fox, Engadget, and the OLC primary) to put the source block well above our two-source floor. What the opinion does not do remains as important as what it does: it does not declare TikTok safe or compel any agency to act.
